title: Modify Registry
summary: The Windows Registry is a hierarchical configuration store, and modifying it is rarely an end in itself: it is how an adversary makes another technique survive, hide or take effect. Values can be written locally with the built in reg utility, through the Windows API from a remote access tool, or over the network when the remote registry service and administrative access are available. Common aims include establishing autostart persistence, weakening defences such as macro restrictions, adjusting behaviour so elevation or outbound requests are permitted, storing encoded payloads or configuration data, and hiding keys by using names that begin with a null character so ordinary tools fail to read them. The registry also holds long lived state, so malicious changes can outlast the process that made them. Detection relies on registry auditing, Sysmon registry value set events, and monitoring of the autostart locations that decide what runs at logon, boot or scheduled times. Legitimate software writes these keys constantly, so reviewers must weigh context and history rather than treat every change as hostile.

beginner.definition: The Windows Registry is a central store of settings that Windows and installed programs read. It holds rules for how the system behaves and what starts automatically. This technique means an attacker changes those settings. The change can make their software run again later or weaken a protection.
beginner.whyItMatters: Malicious settings survive a restart, so a problem you thought you fixed can come straight back. Some changes quietly switch off safety features, such as the block on macros in office documents. Others hide data where few people look. The registry also changes all the time for normal reasons, so real problems can blend into routine noise.
howItWorks: The attacker reaches the registry with a built in command line tool, a script or their own software.
Access levels matter, so some keys need administrator rights before they can be written.
An autostart entry is added so the attacker's program runs again after logon or reboot.
Defensive settings are weakened, for example office macro rules or outbound request limits.
Encoded data or configuration is stored in a value instead of a file on disk.
Key names may be crafted with hidden characters so common tools fail to display them.
beginner.example: Every flat in a building shares one rulebook kept at the front desk. A visitor adds a new line saying the desk should hand over spare keys on request. Nothing about the book looks damaged, and staff simply follow the rule from then on. The rule stays in place every day, long after the visitor has gone.
takeaways: Registry changes are how many other techniques become permanent, so they deserve review.
Watch the autostart keys and any change that switches a security setting off.
Baseline normal changes per machine, because the registry is never static.

objectives: Describe what the Windows Registry stores and how it is structured into keys and values.
Explain why attackers modify the registry for persistence, defence evasion and execution.
Identify telemetry sources that record registry changes, including audit settings and Sysmon registry events.
Explain how hidden or oddly named keys can be concealed from common administrative tools.
Distinguish malicious registry modification from routine software configuration changes.
